“Subhūti, if one practices the karma of emptiness, meaninglessness, and desirelessness in accordance with emptiness, and does not exert oneself in practicing emptiness—this is most fitting for the Benefactor of the Multitudes; such a person should receive food.”

If one gives rise to the thought of seeking blessings from the multitude of sages, one immediately follows deception and does not follow the Great Sage; if one causes a worthy person to fail to complete their accumulation of blessings, yet those blessings are neither diminished nor lost, and they uphold the meaning of the Dharma without advancing or retreating, only then should they accept food.
At that time, Subhūti extended his right arm, prostrated in salutation, and proclaimed these words:
"What the elder sister has now spoken is most sincere; it shall be practiced accordingly. Just as you have spoken, please expound for my sake the discourse on equanimity."
Having said this, he proceeded to receive alms.
At that time, the woman offered food to Subhūti and, proclaiming this teaching, addressed him:
"O Venerable One, it is difficult for those who are worthy of offerings to encounter such an opportunity as to follow this and accept equal alms."

Furthermore, many people in this world are full of self-importance and abandon this equality; for this reason, they fall into hell without attaining purity, yet they maintain firm faith as they receive alms.
Then the devas and humans asked the girl:
"By what causes and conditions do you understand all dharmas and practice them with your mind?
The girl replied:
"What do you think, O devas?
Do you perceive my body as that of a man?
What is it that I practice?"
"For this reason, it follows from its original cause.
The deva replied,
"I am not clever enough."
The girl replied:
"Thus it is, O devas!
Constantly practicing the karma that is like an illusion—what 'I' could there be in this body that is manifested?"
Is it not like an echo?
Furthermore, as all devas and humans respond to sentient beings—whether their words be false or true—all these teachings are entirely equal.
Why is this so? Because all speech, words, and various designations are fundamentally non-existent, yet they naturally issue forth as speech.

When he spoke these verses and instructions on the practice of alms-gathering, hundreds of thousands of devas from that assembly attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, free from dust and defilement.
At that time, the elder sister addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"Virtuous one!
After you have gone and finished your meal, you should proceed to the place where the Buddha is; we too shall go there to listen to the sutra."
Then, having received the alms-food, Subhūti departed from the city of Rājagṛha. With a heart filled with joy upon hearing the Dharma and his mind undistracted, he thought to himself:
"In what place shall I set down my bowl of alms-food?"
"May this person of firm faith not fall into the calamity of transgression.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dānadharmadatta who, knowing the beginning and end of the Venerable Subhūti’s thoughts, went to where he was, prostrated at Subhūti’s feet, and then approached him to ask:
"Venerable Subhūti!"
"By means of these offerings, one practices giving; by means of this, through firm faith, one does not engage in disputes.
Subhūti said: "Virtuous son of good family, what precepts do you establish?"
He replied:
"All dharmas are entirely without anything to be received; precepts are all unattainable, and there is likewise no transgression of prohibitions.
Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

I am fond of taking life and have no delight in giving; I am habituated to sexual misconduct, constantly practice false speech, and further commit divisive talk, harsh words, and take pleasure in frivolous chatter. I always harbor anger and resentment, my mind is set on greed and envy, and I constantly fall into wrong views.
"Why is this? For those who engage in any practice are all transgressing the Dharma; it is only by having nothing to practice that one accords with equality.
At that time, Subhūti thought to himself:
“Listen now to the teaching proclaimed by this son of good family; he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva beyond doubt, so I shall surely question him regarding what he has said.”
Then Subhūti asked: "Noble son!
You have bestowed this meal upon me and declared with your own mouth: 'Indeed, O Righteous One, by means of this food—the alms-food given in faith—shall I not fall into the evil destinies? "

After Subhūti had finished eating, he sat in quiet seclusion. Rising in the late afternoon, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and reported in full to the Buddha the Dharma he had inquired about, as well as the various points of resolution he had reached with the elder sister and her daughters.
The World-Honored One told Subhūti:
"You who possess thorough understanding, pay homage to the bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"The mind is fundamentally not clever," the Buddha said.

"There is a bodhisattva named Zhuan-nü (Turning-Woman). She uses this very skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform and enlighten sentient beings. Even if there were great carts throughout the kingdom of Magadha, each holding hundreds of thousands of *hu* filled with mustard seeds, one might still be able to count their quantity; yet, by encouraging and delighting others through skillful means, she transforms women in this world of endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*), causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path in numbers beyond measure, leading them to be born in the heavens or among humans in limitless abundance."

Then that woman’s elder sister, accompanied by five hundred women, went to where the Buddha was; surrounded by her retinue, she departed from the great city of Rājagṛha and arrived at Vulture Peak Mountain, proceeding to the place where the Buddha stayed.
The Buddha saw the women approaching from afar and said to the Venerable Subhūti, "Do you see them?
Five hundred women are coming together."
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“I see them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Surrounded by her retinue of five hundred women, she proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, went out to meet the woman, and paid homage to her with palms joined.
The woman first prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"Virtuous One, what noble and holy dharma have you attained such that you adopt a stance contrary to the meaning of a noble and holy one, by instead going out to welcome this woman, prostrating, and paying her homage?"
Then the woman said to Śāriputra,
"What do you think, worthy one?
Which of those in the world are noble sages, and who are not noble sages?"
"And yet you have uttered such meaningless words as these.
Śāriputra said, "Sister,
do you know whether those who are sages and worthies in the world are truly sages and worthies?"
The woman replied,
"I fully understand both the holy and the unholy.
Śāriputra said:
"What do you mean?
His daughter replied, "Yes, Śāriputra!"
Those who do not sever the teachings of the noble ones, who do not transgress or lose sight of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, are called noble ones (ārya).
Those who possess gentleness, harmony, and a compassionate heart, and whose practice is not that of ordinary beings but is directed toward liberation, are called noble ones.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there is a woman whose body is adorned with various jewels, who wears pure garments and rare ornaments, perfumes herself with incense, and anoints her body with blended fragrances; who practices wearing these various robes and entertains herself with the five kinds of music, yet does not abandon or deviate from the mind of omniscience—she is most truly noble and holy. She surpasses the eight liberations and the nine successive stages of meditative concentration of the śrāvakas, and excels all arhats who dwell in constant tranquility."

Therefore, Śāriputra, I shall provide you with an analogy so that you may understand this meaning: if one were to place a crystal gem in a vessel of lapis lazuli, and another were to place a moon-pearl in a vessel of clay or wood, which of these would be superior?
Śāriputra replied,
“It is better to place a moon-pearl in a vessel of clay or wood than to place a crystal gem in a vessel of lapis lazuli.
The girl replied:

"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra! If there is a woman who delights in the five pleasures, adorns her body with all manner of jewels, yet establishes the mind upon omniscience (sarvajñatā), she is most exceedingly noble and holy, surpassing the arhat who dwells in the eight liberations, the meditative concentrations, and in tranquility."
Śāriputra asked the girl,
"Sister, do you not aspire to establish yourself in the Mahāyāna?
The girl replied:
"That which is the Great Vehicle neither abides anywhere nor regresses.
He asked again:
"If the Great Vehicle neither abides anywhere nor regresses, how does one train in it?"
The girl replied: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Mahāyāna do not exhaust their ignorance when they set their minds on seeking the Way."
Why is this? Because the Mahāyāna is equal;

that which is inexhaustible consists of the inexhaustibility of ignorance, as well as old age, sickness, and death. Phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished; that which has arisen must inevitably return to extinction, whereas that which is unproduced does not undergo extinction.
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
For one who understands in this way, the twelve links of dependent origination are no longer subject to cessation.
Then Śāriputra asked the girl:
"All the devas and those in the world above should prostrate themselves and pay homage to you as their elder sister; how much more so now, Subhūti?
Then Śāriputra stepped forward and asked the Buddha, "From this day forward, people must not judge one another by outward appearance."
"Why is this? Now, this woman has adorned her body with such ornaments and her eloquence and noble realization are as magnificent as this.
The woman replied:
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
This is not the eloquence of one adorned with ornaments and necklaces.
He asked again:
"What is it? The woman of eloquence replied, "A bodhisattva has eight kinds of ornaments and necklaces;
by adorning his body with these ornaments, his mind becomes pure like space, and through this, the bodhisattva achieves unimpeded, true, and correct eloquence."
What are these eight?
Cultivating the conduct of a bodhisattva without abandoning the mind of enlightenment is the adornment of a bodhisattva;
resolving to embrace the Mahāyāna without clinging to minor details is the establishment of adornment.
Equanimity toward all sentient beings is the adornment of non-harming;
diligence and extensive learning are the adornment of tirelessness;
and being able to immediately practice and uphold the Dharma as it has been heard is the bodily adornment of a bodhisattva.
Adorning the body by resolving the profound and subtle Dharma and thoroughly understanding all dependent origination;
adorning as a bodhisattva by awakening to the faculties of sentient beings;
and adorning as a bodhisattva by that which is established by the Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva’s transformation and edification is the adornment of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Śāriputra, these are the eight matters of adornment practiced by the Bodhisattva; dwelling in these, the Bodhisattva attains unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and transforms all beings obscured within the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*).
Then Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"From which buddha-field did this woman pass away to be born here in this land?
At that moment, the woman transformed herself into another woman, beautiful and exquisite, who stood before Śāriputra and asked:
“Śāriputra! For this reason I ask you:
‘From which land did this woman pass away to arrive here in this land?’”
Śāriputra said: “This woman appearing now is merely a manifested transformation. Such transformations are spontaneous; that which is manifested as a transformation neither perishes nor is born.”
The girl replied: “It is so, Śāriputra!
All dharmas have the natural characteristic of being transformations; it is because of this that the Tathāgata attained supreme perfect enlightenment.”

If one understands that all phenomena are like transformations and possess the nature of spontaneity, then there is neither birth nor passing away; such noble beings possess wisdom as vast as space, and one should not ask:
"From where did they come to be born, or how do they pass away?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"This is the bodhisattva named Parivartakastrī (She Who Turns into a Woman). Having passed away from the world-system of Wondrous Joy under the Buddha Akṣobhya, she has come to be born here. Desiring to transform and enlighten all sentient beings, she manifests in the body of a woman through the power of skillful means."

This Bodhisattva Turning-Woman has, from beginning to end, exhorted and guided countless, immeasurable, and limitless classes of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalāvatī, still in the form of a woman, stepped forward to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and spoke these words:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"

Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, I shall not rise from the ground until I have received my prediction of enlightenment; in the future, may I attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path, and cause this female body to vanish and be transformed into that of a man.
Then the five hundred women prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each sighed, saying:
“We bow our heads again and again; indeed, World-Honored One!
We shall not rise until we have received the prediction of our future enlightenment. May we cast off these female forms and become men, so that we may attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.”

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled; as is the natural auspicious response of the fundamental dharma of all Buddhas, countless colors—blue, yellow, white, black, red, and purple—issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions, circling three times around them, and then re-entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
"Since you laughed, there must have been an intention behind it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Did you see this Bodhisattva Turning-Woman and her five hundred followers prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, weary of their female forms?"
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, I see them. The Buddha said:

"This Bodhisattva Woman-Transformed has already transcended the calculation of kalpas and attained the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way; she shall become a Most Perfectly Awakened One, named King of Repeated Radiance (Prabhāsa-guru-rāja), and will thus achieve the Buddha-way."

The five hundred women were transformed into men and became five hundred bodhisattvas. They were always accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bodhisattvas, having attained *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence. Adorning their bodies with various transformed necklaces and ornaments, they likewise followed the example of this Bodhisattva Turning-Woman (*Nartṛ-bodhisattva*), transforming and adorning their bodies to convert and deliver the multitudes; they also took as their model the Tathāgata King of Radiant Sovereignty (*Prabhāsa-guru-rāja*).
The Tathāgata King of Radiant Layers shall all receive their prediction that they will attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

In the buddha-field of the Tathāgata King of Radiant Layers, there will be abundant prosperity and great peace; the five grains will be extremely cheap, and it will be secure and blissful. The population will flourish, with gods and humans filling the realm; dwellings, palaces, food, and drink will arise spontaneously through transformation, just like in the Tuṣita Heaven.
In that Buddha-land, there is not even the name "woman," much less the existence of a physical form.

All the assembly of bodhisattvas are born by transformation, sitting naturally upon lotus flowers made of the seven treasures; they purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, adorning their bodies with these eight dharmas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Parivartakā and the five hundred women, having heard the Buddha bestow their prophecy, were filled with such spontaneous joy that they leapt into the air at a height of seven fathoms from the ground. Spontaneously, their ages became like those of twelve-year-old boys; none failed to see that they were no longer female in appearance. Descending from the void, they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Buddha.
Then the Buddha stroked their heads with his hand, and immediately they all attained the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this sūtra; uphold, recite, read, and explain it for others."
Ānanda said: “Yes! I shall receive and proclaim it.”
Furthermore, what is the name of this sutra-dharma?
How should it be venerated and titled?
The Buddha said:
"It is titled 'The Chapter on Skillful Means in Accordance with Circumstances: The Prediction Bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Who Transformed from Female. You should uphold it.
Ānanda replied again, "Yes, sir;
I accept your command."
Thus the Buddha spoke.

The venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Turned-Woman, the assembly of five hundred, and all those present in the gathering—devas, humans, gandharvas, and asuras—heard what the Buddha had said and were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Scripture on Accordance with Expedient Means, Scroll II.
